title: Assigning Animations
principle: Specify every animation's length and attack timing up front
why: Communicating animation ideas to the team is vital, and he sets timings that feel right with the game's push and pull in mind before animators start.
how: Write an animation list describing each movement in text with its length and when the attack occurs; mark loops like idle and walk as 'Loop' or 'Any'.
example: Super Smash Bros. fighter animation lists.
quote: I also note animation length, as well as when the attack itself occurs.

title: Assigning Animations
principle: Let animators fill gaps while keeping the character's appeal first
why: A figure's range of motion is far lower than an in-game model's, so animators must fill gaps and work out details; some ideas don't go as planned and may be let go.
how: Treat the spec as a first step, be willing to drop ideas that don't work, and judge results by whether the character shines.
anti_pattern: Treating the director's spec as the finished animation.
quote: I always take extra care to try and make the character shine and offer the best game experience possible.

title: Too Much is Just Right
principle: Exaggerate attack poses until they nearly break the rig.
why: Attacks are small on a small screen, so the usual problem is not going far enough; if a pose looks OK, there's room to go further.
how: Push twists and extensions past natural limits, and build flexible rigs (moving shoulders, independent upper and lower body) that allow it.
anti_pattern: Keeping poses within the physically possible.
example: Kazuya's Roundhouse to Triple Spin Kick; Virtua Fighter's opposed upper and lower body.
quote: Animation that pushes your rig's weighting to the breaking point is good animation.

title: Too Much is Just Right
principle: Judge animation in motion, not by warped-looking paused frames.
why: Correcting a model that looks warped when the action is stopped kills the energy of the animation.
how: Review attacks at full speed and in-game size, and reject fixes for distortions that only show up in freeze-frames.
anti_pattern: Smoothing out deformations that are only visible when paused.
quote: Sometimes a model looks warped when the action is stopped, and we're asked to make corrections, but that really kills the energy of the animation.

title: Too Much is Just Right
principle: Overshoot the target pose, then pull back on the next frame.
why: Going past the natural limit and then pulling back makes even linear animation livelier; he has used it since the NES days.
how: In a frame sequence, place one frame beyond the final pose and settle back to that pose on the following frame.
example: Kirby's Adventure's Needle ability, where frame three goes too far and frame four pulls back.
quote: This also works with linear animations— go over the natural limit, then pull back a bit.

title: Breaking Down Attack Animations
principle: Snap to a big lead-in pose on the attack's first frame.
why: A smooth transition from standby takes too long; an instant big pose tells the player the input registered and cues the opponent to dodge.
how: Skip easing frames out of standby and make frame one of the attack a big windup pose.
anti_pattern: Gradual transitions into the windup.
quote: By instantly jumping to a big pose, the player can immediately know their input was recognized.

title: Breaking Down Attack Animations
principle: Hold a distinct follow-through, then let cancel frames return control.
why: The follow-through is the opening when the player can't act, so it must read clearly; returning control only at standby felt heavy or rigid.
how: Make the follow-through look clearly unlike standby and hold it, and add cancel frames so players can move, jump or attack early.
anti_pattern: Returning control only once the character is back in standby.
example: Smash Bros. through Melee, before cancel frames.
quote: The player can't control the character here, so we keep this pose very distinct from the standby pose, and hold it as long as possible.

title: Eight Hit Stop Techniques
principle: Blend into damage poses and keep the attacker creeping during hit stop
why: A victim who freezes or snaps into one pose looks stiff; blending over about four frames gives a fluid, satisfying result. A barely moving attacker makes swords look like they're actually cutting.
how: Interpolate the victim into the damage pose across about four frames of hit stop. Advance the attacker's animation so slowly it doesn't move every frame, then resume normally, with a per-attack toggle.
anti_pattern: Freezing the victim in place or snapping straight to the damage pose.
example: A sword fighter's strong swing in Smash Bros. Ultimate: the tip keeps inching upward during hit stop
quote: the motion is smoothly blended across four or so frames, giving a fluid, satisfying result.

title: Making Lead-ins Instant and Impactful
principle: Snap to the lead-in pose the instant the button is pressed
why: In Smash, responsiveness comes first. Lag from networks or TVs can't be fully removed, but players can be told immediately that their input was received.
how: Skip interpolation from the standby pose: on the first frame after input, show a drastically different lead-in pose. For charge attacks, hold that pose and shake in place.
anti_pattern: Interpolating smoothly from standby to avoid an animation skip, which delays visible feedback.
example: Charging a Smash Attack in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate
quote: There's no way to completely eliminate lag from network or TV problems, but we can let players know right away that their input was received.

title: Making Lead-ins Instant and Impactful
principle: Size each windup for impact and lag cover, not just speed
why: A game doesn't need lead-ins to work, and instant attacks feel responsive, but a big windup gives visual impact and helps hide network lag online.
how: Give light, spammable moves no lead-in (the hit comes one frame after input) and heavy moves a big, readable windup, always judging the input response.
anti_pattern: Making every attack as quick as possible.
example: Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack (out one frame after input); Final Fight's instant jab
quote: So just making them as quick as possible isn't always going to be the best solution.

title: Attack Poses
principle: Design the hit-stop frame as the attack's key pose
why: Hit stop freezes the instant an attack connects, so that pose tends to be the most memorable, and attack animations affect fun more than any others.
how: Include the moment of contact in animation references and review it on its own; for sword swings, start hit stop once the blade has swung out a bit.
anti_pattern: Starting hit stop before the sword has swung, which loses the "hit" feeling.
example: Smash Bros. hit stop poses
quote: The poses in that moment tend to be the most memorable, so it's important to get them right.

title: Attack Poses
principle: Give every hit pose a distinct silhouette from the gameplay view
why: Smash is viewed from the side, so profile silhouettes matter most, and a minor silhouette tweak can make a huge difference.
how: Make all four limbs clearly visible in profile, and check the pose on both the left and right of the screen.
example: Pyra's pose before and after Sakurai's feedback
quote: One minor tweak to the silhouette can make a huge difference.

title: Attack Poses
principle: Exaggerate, twist and avoid symmetry in attack poses
why: Exaggeration helps movement read from far away, and symmetrical poses or plain sideways bends look far less interesting than a twist.
how: Push poses further than feels natural, break symmetry unless it's deliberately comic, and add torso twist instead of a simple side bend.
anti_pattern: Completely symmetrical poses; simply bending torsos to the side.
quote: As a general rule, you want to exaggerate. This will help your movement read more clearly even from far away.

title: Attack Poses
principle: Keep attacks on the gameplay plane so hits register
why: If attacks stray toward or away from the screen, the hits may not register correctly.
how: Keep attack motion centered in the plane where collision happens rather than angling it toward or away from the camera.
anti_pattern: Attacks that drift toward or away from the screen.
quote: Keep your attacks centered. If they stray toward or away from the screen, the hits may not register correctly.

title: Follow-Throughs Make the Impact
principle: Animate recovery as a big, weighty motion, not a blend to idle
why: The hit itself ends in a fraction of a second, so the follow-through is what shows players what the character just did and how heavy it was.
how: Keep the motion going as long as possible with large movements that carry the strike's momentum before returning to standby.
anti_pattern: Interpolating straight from the hit back to the standby pose.
quote: The follow-through after an attack determines the impact of the attack itself. Don't let it fizzle out—keep those actions expressive right to the end.

title: Units of Speed
principle: Stylize locomotion when speed outruns a natural walk cycle
why: Pit moved so fast that normally animated legs could never keep up.
how: For very fast movement, use bounding or sliding motions instead of a sped-up realistic leg cycle.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising gave Pit a bounding motion and let him slide along the ground.
quote: If we animated him normally, his legs would never keep up— so we instead gave him more of a bounding motion, and let him slide along the ground.

title: Exaggerate to Make Up for Information Loss
principle: Exaggerate animations to make up for information game characters lack
why: Game characters lose a wide range of the information real humans offer, and no part of them truly exists, so 'too much' is 'just right'.
how: Push poses, arcs and accents beyond realistic levels in both cutscenes and gameplay, and make a sword swing more than just a swing.
anti_pattern: Literal, realistic motions that come up short where it matters.
example: Clock Tower 3's over-the-top cutscenes, directed by Kinji Fukasaku.
quote: With polygon-based characters, you lose a wide range of information that real humans offer, so you have to make up for that with big performances.

title: Exaggerate to Make Up for Information Loss
principle: Push motion capture bigger instead of using it raw
why: Motion capture data generally can't be dropped straight into a game and work; going really big tends to look best.
how: Treat capture as a starting point and exaggerate it before it ships.
anti_pattern: Dropping mocap straight into the game.
quote: When you're using motion capture to make animations, you generally can't drop that data straight into the game and have it work.

title: Exaggerate to Make Up for Information Loss
principle: Scale exaggeration to the character's on-screen size
why: Motion that works up close feels far too understated when the character is small or far away.
how: Review animations at the real gameplay camera distance and size, and exaggerate further where they read as weak.
anti_pattern: Judging animations only in close-up views.
quote: Stay mindful of your character's screen presence, size, and controls, then go big to let those animations really pack a punch!

title: Posing Suggestions
principle: Practice posing with a physical action figure
why: Having a physical object to reference teaches a great deal about what makes a pose cool and which angle works best.
how: Keep a posable figure at hand, pose it and zoom it around (bundodo) to train your eye.
example: Pit figma figure.
quote: If you want to develop an eye for posing, there's no better way than to toy with a physical figure

title: Posing Suggestions
principle: Break symmetry and straight lines to make poses dynamic
why: A figure stood up normally isn't terribly exciting; asymmetry and varied lines make it dashing.
how: Avoid left-right symmetry and straight-on facing, lower the chin, tilt the head off right angles, and give torso, hips and legs different lines (an S curve).
anti_pattern: Symmetrical, front-facing standing poses.
example: Pit figma: default vs. adjusted standing pose.

title: Posing Suggestions
principle: Shape arms, wrists and feet with the silhouette in mind
why: Small limb details change how cool a pose reads, even on a stationary figure.
how: Set arms at different bent angles close to the torso, bend wrists slightly forward, shift the center of gravity off-middle, and angle feet outward at different camera depths.
anti_pattern: Arms far from the torso and wrists as straight extensions of the arms.

title: Squashing and Scaling
principle: Use squash and stretch to give objects texture and life
why: Rotation and translation are commonplace, but adding scaling makes a bouncing ball feel totally different, almost touchable; it can really punch up animation.
how: Add squash to landings, crouches and bounces, then compare the animation with and without scaling.
anti_pattern: Treating rotation and translation as the whole toolkit.
example: A bouncing-ball GIF shown with and without scaling; Kirby's crouch and landing squash since Game Boy.

title: Squashing and Scaling
principle: Preserve volume: widen whenever you squash
why: Keeping mass roughly constant sells the squash; when 3D Kirby was only squashed vertically he lost physical presence, so Sakurai asked for more volume on the sides.
how: Stretch horizontally when squashing vertically; on 3D models shape a squashed pose (oval-track profile, or a blend shape) instead of just scaling one axis.
anti_pattern: Squashing on one axis only, so the shape loses volume and looks dull.
example: Kirby's 3D model, per a Daily Report image asking for side volume.
quote: A key rule to follow with this technique is to always keep the object's mass roughly the same.

title: Damage Animations
principle: Make the first damage frame an extreme pain pose unlike standby
why: Hitstop freezes that first frame, so it's what players actually see. An extreme pose that's nothing like standby makes the hit readable even from far away.
how: Author the hitstop frame as an exaggerated pain pose and blend into it briefly from the pose at impact instead of snapping.
anti_pattern: Damage poses that resemble the idle/standby pose.
example: Smash Bros. damage reactions. Kirby's extreme damage pose drawn in the Kirby Super Star design document.
quote: The damage pose and standby pose can be quite similar in some games, but we like to go for something more extreme that's nothing like the standby pose.

title: Damage Animations
principle: Break symmetry and twist bodies so hit reactions read as silhouettes
why: Twisting the body lets the arms and legs read clearly, which wouldn't happen if the character just flew sideways, so both players feel the impact.
how: In every damage and knockback pose, rotate the torso against the hips and separate the limbs from the body outline.
anti_pattern: Stiff, symmetric, side-on knockback poses.
example: Smash Bros. knockback animations.
quote: For all our damage animations, we emphasize breaking a character's symmetry and making their silhouette clearly legible.

title: Damage Animations
principle: Choose damage reactions by impact height and hit strength
why: Picking the reaction closest to the point of impact, scaled by strength, makes each hit look like it landed where and how hard it did.
how: Build high/middle/low reactions selected by the nearest impact point, each in small/medium/large strengths on the ground (nine total), plus a separate knockback set.
anti_pattern: One generic flinch for every hit.
example: Smash Bros.' nine ground damage reaction types.

title: Damage Animations
principle: Check hit-reaction stance changes don't shove targets out of combos
why: Changing a character's stance on hit can move their top node, so a target may slide backward and the rest of a combo misses.
how: Test multi-hit strings against every reaction stance and correct root/top-node offsets so targets stay in place.
anti_pattern: Letting the animation's root motion drift the target away during a combo.
example: Smash Bros.: a neutral attack combo missing because the hit fighter moved back.

title: The Perils of Interpolation
principle: Reach key poses fast and minimize interpolated in-between frames
why: Tools interpolate conveniently, but interpolated frames overpower the key poses and make an animation feel slow even when its frame count matches the original.
how: Scrub interpolated attacks and cut in-between time so key frames arrive quickly, judging snappiness by eye rather than frame count.
anti_pattern: Accepting default interpolation between reference poses.
example: An 8-frame kick in Smash Ultimate that felt slow when interpolated and much snappier in the release version, at the same 8 frames.
quote: But convenience doesn't mean quality.

title: The Perils of Interpolation
principle: Hold the anticipation, then snap through key poses
why: Saving time for the lead-in and attack keeps momentum. Key poses shown for even one frame each still leave an impression when the attack hits.
how: Pull the wind-up further back, hold it relatively long, then pass through each key pose in as little as one frame.
anti_pattern: Spreading time evenly across the motion.
example: Ryu's crouching heavy punch in Smash Ultimate: forearm pulled back, long-held anticipation, three original key poses on screen one frame each.
quote: Make sure your animations really come out swinging!

title: The Perils of Interpolation
principle: Exaggerate key poses beyond the source material
why: Moving from 2D to 3D loses momentum, so poses need more energy than the original key frames to feel as strong.
how: When adapting reference art, push each key pose further, e.g., a deeper wind-up or a different first frame for more momentum.
anti_pattern: Copying the source poses exactly and expecting the same punch.
example: Ryu's first frame differs in Smash to express more momentum than his crouching start.
quote: If possible, try to give the poses even more energy than the original key frames.

title: The Perils of Interpolation
principle: Give follow-through its own path, distinct from the standby pose
why: The original's backwards playback doesn't translate to 3D, and a follow-through that matches standby loses the motion's character.
how: Animate a separate return trajectory after the strike, kept close to the original's feel, that doesn't simply end at idle.
anti_pattern: Reversing the attack animation or ending on the standby pose.
example: Ryu's uppercut follow-through in Smash Ultimate.
quote: You don't want your follow-through to be the same as your standby pose.

title: Special Crossover! #2
principle: Add recoil animation to weapons every time they fire
why: Sakurai singles out Star Force's missile recoil, where the side cannons pull back on every shot, along with its beautiful 5-frame explosion, as details that make the shooting feel great.
how: On each shot, snap the gun or cannon back for a few frames and return it; author explosions as short, deliberate frame sequences.
example: Star Force — side cannons pull back with each missile; 5-frame explosion
quote: Whenever you fire missiles, you get this bam, bam, bam kind of recoil animation.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising
principle: Make collision and animation agree so hits look and feel right
why: Attacks that look like they should hit but don't, or that keep hitting after the swing, feel wrong; Sakurai fixes both collision and animation.
how: When a hit feels off, adjust hitbox shape and timing together with the animation's arc or pose until the visual and the collision match.
anti_pattern: Hit visuals and collision that disagree.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Pyra's forward aerial collision shortened; Mythra's slash aligned to a diagonal
quote: A common issue: attacks that look like they should hit, but don't.

title: Facial Animations
principle: Push facial expressions past 'done', because CG loses information
why: Smash faces are small and need no lip sync, yet most incoming artwork had expression shifts that were too small; since CG loses information, too much is about right for realistic and cartoony styles alike.
how: Once an expression looks finished, exaggerate it one more step and judge it in-game at real viewing size.
anti_pattern: Subtle expressions on characters seen at small sizes.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Wolf's damage face retouch
quote: Get it to where it feels done, then go a step further and make the movements even bigger.

title: Facial Animations
principle: Build expressions on anatomy: eye whites, offset teeth, jaw structure
why: Sakurai's details include visible eye whites above and below on wide-open eyes and teeth that aren't directly aligned; Wolf's damage face was emphasized to suit a wolf's jaw.
how: For shocked faces show eye white above and below the iris, offset upper and lower teeth, and size mouth shapes to the character's jaw.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Wolf's damage face
quote: Making the whites of wide-open eyes visible at both the top and the bottom or making sure the upper and lower teeth aren't directly aligned

title: Facial Animations
principle: When the source has no facial range, express emotion through movement
why: Steve's only facial animation is a blink, so his other movements must make up for it; putting the source material first matters more than adding faces.
how: Keep faithful but limited faces as they are and give those characters more expressive body motion instead.
anti_pattern: Inventing facial expressions the source character never had.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Steve only blinks
quote: We do have to make up for that with his other movements, but that's all part of putting the source material first.

title: Blade Trails
principle: Adjust swing animations until the trail reads from the camera
why: A fast blade's raw path looks angular, and trails can be almost imperceptible when viewed from the side.
how: Check swings from the gameplay camera and correct the animation so the arc stands out; avoid plain horizontal slashes.
anti_pattern: A plain horizontal slash whose trail vanishes from the side.

title: Flipped Animation
principle: Mirror animations so characters face the camera from both sides
why: Without mirroring, the character on the right faces away, so you can't see their expression and get little information.
how: Use mirrored poses and movements when a character changes facing in a side view instead of turning the model around.
anti_pattern: Expressive characters showing their backs on one side of the screen.
example: Smash Bros. adopted flipped animation after Brawl; Street Fighter IV kept Street Fighter II's sprite mirroring.
quote: We can't see his expression, and receive little information. For someone this expressive, he should really be facing us, right?

title: Flipped Animation
principle: Budget for the handedness problems mirroring creates
why: Mirroring takes a lot of work: right-handed punches become left-handed and held items must switch hands.
how: Plan quick hand swaps for items and accept flipped handedness; skip mirroring for characters without horizontal symmetry, such as sword fighters.
anti_pattern: Mirroring asymmetric sword fighters.

title: Flipped Animation
principle: Angle side-view poses toward the camera to show the face
why: Pure profile views aren't fun to look at and hide the face for half of the movement.
how: Turn runs and similar moves diagonally toward the viewer so the face and visual information stay visible from the side camera.
anti_pattern: Animating runs directly from the side.
example: Kirby's run in Smash Bros. faces diagonally so his face shows from the side view.

title: Animation Blending
principle: Blend into the next animation on cancels instead of snapping
why: Blending lets the same follow-up animation start naturally from drastically different poses.
how: When an input arrives during cancel frames, blend from the current pose of the canceled action into the new animation.
anti_pattern: Hard snaps from one animation to the next.
example: In Smash Bros., idle-to-walk and attack-to-walk both look natural despite very different starting poses.

title: Animation Blending
principle: Keep blends short so animation keeps its rhythm and impact
why: Making animation too smooth decreases rhythm and impact, and automated blending can distort the motion.
how: Set short blend durations and appropriate strength, and check blends for distorted poses.
anti_pattern: Long, overly smooth blends.
quote: As a result, you don't want a blend to last too long. Make it quick and snappy.

title: Animation Blending
principle: Use positional blending for directional and terrain-aware motion
why: Directional inputs and 3D terrain create too many pose combinations to animate by hand.
how: Blend a center stance with poses around a circle for directional moves, and in 3D, blend upper and lower body separately and adapt legs and turns to terrain.
example: Smash Bros. shield shifting blends circular movement with the fixed center stance.

title: Portraying Fingers
principle: Pose swung objects in a diagonal grip, not perpendicular to fingers
why: A perpendicular grip suits simply holding something, but swinging with the forearm uses a diagonal grip, and a perpendicular one makes characters look like action figures.
how: Review every weapon or tool hold, and angle the fingers and the object diagonally for anything that gets swung.
anti_pattern: Rigid perpendicular grips on swung weapons.
quote: if you're going to swing it along with your forearm, you use a diagonal grip.

title: Always Keep Attack Collision in Mind
principle: Line up the strongest attack pose with the first active collision frame
why: The clean-hit frame is where hitstop happens and players get a clear view, and on finishing blows the screen stops completely, so a weak pose there looks bad.
how: Start collision partway through a swing, once the pose is strong, rather than at the first frame of motion.
anti_pattern: Collision that starts during a weak wind-up pose.
example: Smash Bros. sword swings: collision doesn't start until the sword is partway through the swing.
quote: Weak attack poses are no good in these situations.

title: Always Keep Attack Collision in Mind
principle: Keep attack animations positioned where the collision actually is
why: A designer can make any animation connect, but a large gap between visuals and collision feels broken; some mismatch is fine if it makes the game more fun.
how: Have animators work with hitbox timing and placement visible, and review attacks with collision displayed.
anti_pattern: Fixing a misplaced animation by stretching the hitbox to meet it.
quote: When crafting attack animations, it's important that the animators are always aware of when and where collision occurs.

title: Manga-like Visuals
principle: Swap mouth cels for profile lip movement instead of animating jaws
why: Moving the mouth by swapping cels is easier to produce and may make mouth movement easier to read.
how: Use texture or cel swaps for the mouth in profile shots rather than rigging jaw motion.
example: Mega Man Legends shows mouth movement in profile by swapping cels without animating the jaw.

title: The Limitations of Skeletons
principle: Push key poses beyond realistic joint limits for extra oomph
why: Pushing beyond common sense is what gives animation its greatness, and bending past a straight arm adds oomph.
how: Try extending limbs past straight in strong attack poses and check whether your rig allows it.
anti_pattern: Stopping at realistic joint limits by default.
quote: In any case, I'd say that pushing beyond common sense is what gives animation its greatness.

title: The Limitations of Skeletons
principle: Plan rigs for cartoon exaggeration at the start of development
why: Joints that bend backward are harder to use (IK may flip), and fixes like extra joints add processing load and need cartoon-minded animators.
how: Decide early if the style needs exaggeration, then budget for extra joints and brief or hire animators with cartoon sensibilities.
example: Sakurai suggested exaggerated rigs at the start of Smash Bros. development, but processing load and staffing left it unsolved.

title: Establishing Characters Through Their Design
principle: Pose characters to express who they are
why: Depending on how well they're posed, the same character can look and feel completely different.
how: Review each character's key poses and rework any that don't convey their personality.

title: Rotation on Two Axes
principle: Rotate organic motion on two axes, never just one
why: A head turned only around the Y axis feels mechanical and a one-axis wrist twist looks like a drill; tilting a bit before turning is more believable.
how: Layer a dip (X axis) or tilt (Z axis) onto every Y-axis turn of heads, wrists and torsos.
anti_pattern: Pure single-axis rotation on characters.
example: Sakurai's own head turn, shown first on one axis.
quote: When creating human movement, make it a point to rotate on two axes.

title: Rotation on Two Axes
principle: Move connected joints along with the rotating part
why: Connected parts move in reality: the shoulder and collarbone work in tandem with the wrist.
how: When animating a twist such as revving a motorcycle, shift the shoulder and collarbone along with the wrist.
example: Revving a motorcycle.
quote: The shoulder and collarbone work in tandem with the wrist, for example.

title: Rotation on Two Axes
principle: Hand-tune rotation timing instead of trusting software curves
why: Generated function curves can look believable, but how a rotation reaches its end pose decides its personality.
how: Slightly offset the timing of the two axes, add an occasional counter-motion, and choose a downward, upward or level path on purpose.
anti_pattern: Accepting the 3D software's default function curves as-is.
quote: even rotations that finish in the same place can express drastically different personalities depending on how they reach that point.

title: Rotation on Two Axes
principle: Account for the eye line before finalizing head turns
why: Animators often turn the whole head fully before facial animation exists, and once the eyes are added the turn can be bigger than wanted.
how: Plan eye direction with the head turn, and reduce the head rotation once the eyes carry part of the look.
anti_pattern: Over-turning the head before the eyes are animated.
quote: once the eye line gets added in, that large of a head turn might just end up being a bigger movement than you want.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising: Sora Edition
principle: Check every special move in both its ground and aerial versions
why: Sora's Sonic Blade had drastically different aerial and ground poses, and its distance shrank when attacking upward, a type of bug.
how: Play both versions of every special side by side, comparing poses and reach in each direction.
example: Smash Ultimate, Sora's Sonic Blade.
quote: For special moves, you need to check both the ground and aerial versions.

title: What Happens When You Shift the Center of Gravity?
principle: Offset rotation axes slightly from the object's center
why: Rotating around the exact center feels less organic, while a slightly shifted axis makes the motion a little erratic and expressive.
how: Move the pivot of spinning items and swung weapons off the geometric center or grip, and compare it with the centered version.
example: Smash Ultimate's bomb throw; Pyra's Blazing End, whose axis was moved off the sword's grip.
quote: But the axis of rotation is shifted slightly away from the center of the bomb. It makes the movement feel a little erratic.

title: What Happens When You Shift the Center of Gravity?
principle: Don't let software defaults decide how things move
why: Designers are used to straight lines and smooth circles, but animation means putting a soul into something unmoving, and defaults look bland.
how: Review linear moves and center-point rotations in your game and give each some personality, using quick mock-ups during reviews.
anti_pattern: Straight lines and smooth circles left as the software makes them.
quote: try to find ways to avoid the blandness that can come from simply following your software's tendencies.
